claim: Over 20 million single- and double-mutant budding yeast strains were generated in the SGA dataset.
source: In the SGA dataset, over 20 million single- and double-mutant budding yeast strains were generated.
evidence: Direct statement about the size of the SGA dataset.

claim: Colony growth rates of mutant yeast strains were measured in SGAs (Tong et al., 2001; Baryshnikova et al., 2010b; Costanzo et al., 2010; Costanzo et al., 2016).
source: Then, the growth rates of their colonies were measured in SGAs (Tong et al., 2001; Baryshnikova et al., 2010b; Costanzo et al., 2010; Costanzo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work describing the SGA methodology.

claim: Each mutant's fitness was defined as the measured growth rate normalized by that of the wild-type strain.
source: Each mutant's fitness was then defined as this measured growth rate normalized by that of the wild-type strain, enabling a consistent comparison across thousands of genotypes.
evidence: Direct statement of the definition used in the study.

claim: The Product neutrality function predicts that the fitness of a double mutant is the product of the fitnesses of the two corresponding single mutants.
source: The Product neutrality function predicts that the fitness of a double mutant is the product of the fitnesses of the two corresponding single mutants, while the Additive neutrality function proposes that the difference between the double-mutant and wild-type fitnesses is the sum of the differences between the two mutant and wild-type fitnesses.
evidence: Direct definition of the Product neutrality function.

claim: The Additive neutrality function proposes that the difference between the double-mutant and wild-type fitnesses is the sum of the differences between the two mutant and wild-type fitnesses.
source: The Product neutrality function predicts that the fitness of a double mutant is the product of the fitnesses of the two corresponding single mutants, while the Additive neutrality function proposes that the difference between the double-mutant and wild-type fitnesses is the sum of the differences between the two mutant and wild-type fitnesses.
evidence: Direct definition of the Additive neutrality function.

claim: The Minimum neutrality function proposes that the fitness of the double mutant is equal to the fitness of the least fit single mutant.
source: The Minimum neutrality function proposes that the fitness of the double mutant is equal to the fitness of the least fit single mutant.
evidence: Direct definition of the Minimum neutrality function.

claim: The Product neutrality function better predicts double-mutant fitnesses than the Additive or Minimum neutrality functions over a broad range of fitness defects.
source: Consistent with previous work (Mani et al., 2008), we see that the Product neutrality function better predicts double-mutant fitnesses as a function of the single-mutant fitnesses over a broad range of fitness defects (Figure 1, Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: Supported by data analysis shown in figures and consistent with prior work.

claim: For a maximum single-mutant fitness of 72%, the median residual is −0.8% for the Product neutrality function.
source: For instance, for a maximum single-mutant fitness of 72%, the median residual is −0.8% for the Product neutrality function, while they are −16.8% and 9.8% for the Minimum and Additive neutrality functions, respectively.
evidence: Specific quantitative result from data analysis.

claim: For a maximum single-mutant fitness of 72%, the median residual is −16.8% for the Minimum neutrality function.
source: For instance, for a maximum single-mutant fitness of 72%, the median residual is −0.8% for the Product neutrality function, while they are −16.8% and 9.8% for the Minimum and Additive neutrality functions, respectively.
evidence: Specific quantitative result from data analysis.

claim: For a maximum single-mutant fitness of 72%, the median residual is 9.8% for the Additive neutrality function.
source: For instance, for a maximum single-mutant fitness of 72%, the median residual is −0.8% for the Product neutrality function, while they are −16.8% and 9.8% for the Minimum and Additive neutrality functions, respectively.
evidence: Specific quantitative result from data analysis.

claim: At a maximum single-mutant fitness of 72%, the interquartile range of residuals lies between 8% and 10% depending on the neutrality function considered.
source: At a maximum single-mutant fitness of 72%, the interquartile range lies between 8% and 10% depending on the neutrality function considered.
evidence: Specific quantitative result describing variation in the data.

claim: The Product neutrality function best describes double mutant fitnesses for mutations to essential and nonessential genes, and across different temperature conditions.
source: This observation that the Product neutrality function best describes double mutant fitnesses holds for mutations to essential and nonessential genes, and across different temperature conditions (see Methods and Appendix 1—figures 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by data analysis across different experimental conditions.

claim: The Minimum neutrality function generally predicts fitnesses that are too high.
source: The Minimum neutrality function generally predicts fitnesses that are too high, while the Additive neutrality function generally predicts fitnesses that are too low.
evidence: General observation from data analysis.

claim: The Additive neutrality function generally predicts fitnesses that are too low.
source: The Minimum neutrality function generally predicts fitnesses that are too high, while the Additive neutrality function generally predicts fitnesses that are too low.
evidence: General observation from data analysis.

claim: The Product neutrality function is a good description of typical interactions between genes associated with two distinct biological processes.
source: This shows that, while imperfect, the Product neutrality function is a good description of typical interactions, while the Additive and Minimum neutrality functions have large, systematic residuals (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by analysis of GO-annotated biological processes shown in figures.

claim: The Additive and Minimum neutrality functions have large, systematic residuals for interactions between genes associated with two distinct biological processes.
source: This shows that, while imperfect, the Product neutrality function is a good description of typical interactions, while the Additive and Minimum neutrality functions have large, systematic residuals (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by analysis of GO-annotated biological processes shown in figures.

claim: For gene pairs in the same biological process, there are more deviations and significantly larger residuals from the Product neutrality function.
source: Consistent with this notion, for gene pairs in the same biological process, we observe more deviations as well as significantly larger residuals (Appendix 1—figure 3B–D).
evidence: Supported by data analysis shown in appendix figures.

claim: Large residuals (both positive and negative) are significantly more likely for two mutations categorized as being in the same GO process.
source: The quantitative comparison of the two types of interactions reveals that large residuals (both positive and negative) are significantly more likely for two mutations categorized as being in the same GO process (Appendix 1—figure 3E, F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative comparison shown in appendix figures.

claim: Colony growth follows a biphasic pattern with a first exponential phase followed by a slower linear phase as the colony expands.
source: In particular, colony growth has been shown to follow a biphasic pattern (Meunier and Choder, 1999). A first exponential phase is followed by a slower linear phase as the colony expands.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The linear colony-size expansion rate is directly proportional to the square root of the exponential growth rate under non-limiting conditions.
source: More precisely, mathematical models show the linear colony-size expansion rate is directly proportional to the square root of the exponential growth rate under non-limiting conditions.
evidence: Based on mathematical models of colony growth.

claim: Colony growth is dominated by the expansion of the population of cells in an annulus at the colony border that are exposed to rich nutrient conditions.
source: Intuitively, this relationship arises because colony growth is dominated by the expansion of the population of cells in an annulus at the colony border that are exposed to rich nutrient conditions.
evidence: Explanation based on understanding of colony growth dynamics.

claim: Cells in the interior of the colony experience poor nutrient conditions, grow very slowly, and do not contribute to colony growth.
source: In contrast, the cells in the interior of the colony experience poor nutrient conditions, grow very slowly, and do not contribute to colony growth.
evidence: Explanation based on understanding of colony growth dynamics.

claim: From the perspective of the Product neutrality function, fitnesses based on colony expansion rates are equivalent to fitnesses based on single-cell exponential growth rates.
source: In other words, from the perspective of the Product neutrality function, fitnesses based on colony expansion rates are equivalent to fitnesses based on single-cell exponential growth rates.
evidence: Derived from mathematical relationships between colony and single-cell growth rates.

claim: The Scott-Hwa model defines growth as resulting from two sets of processes, metabolic and translational, that interact in a linear pathway.
source: In its simplest form, the model defines growth as resulting from two sets of processes, metabolic and translational, that interact in a linear pathway.
evidence: Description of the Scott-Hwa model structure.

claim: In the Scott-Hwa model, the metabolic sector provides precursors that are then assembled into proteins by the translational sector.
source: The metabolic sector provides precursors that are then assembled into proteins by the translational sector, and the flux through each sector is determined by the amount of proteins in that sector.
evidence: Description of the Scott-Hwa model structure.

claim: The Product neutrality function fits the mutational analysis of the Scott-Hwa model better than the Additive or Minimum neutrality functions.
source: Under this model, which we call Scott–Hwa in reference to the authors of the initial work, we observe that the Product neutrality function fits the mutational analysis of the Scott–Hwa model better than the Additive or Minimum neutrality functions (Figure 3D-G).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of the model shown in figures.

claim: The better performance of the Product neutrality function in the Scott-Hwa model arises from a type of feedback regulation that ensures that the flux through all sectors is equal.
source: We understand the better performance of the Product neutrality function to arise from a type of feedback regulation that ensures that the flux through all sectors is equal.
evidence: Interpretation of the model results based on the model's feedback mechanism.

claim: In the Scott-Hwa model, metabolic and translational sectors are coupled because the cell is assumed to have a feedback process to optimize growth rate under any perturbation to its parameters.
source: In this model, these sectors are coupled because the cell is assumed to have a feedback process to optimize growth rate under any perturbation to its parameters.
evidence: Explanation of the model's feedback mechanism.

claim: If the growth-optimizing feedback in the Scott-Hwa model were absent, the double-mutant fitness would follow a Minimum neutrality function.
source: If this feedback were absent, then the growth rates of the double mutant would be significantly lower. In that case, the double-mutant fitness actually follows a Minimum neutrality function (see Appendix 1 and Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: Supported by analysis of the model without feedback shown in appendix.

claim: The Product neutrality function does not accurately predict model fitnesses well for beneficial mutations in the Scott-Hwa model.
source: Finally, we also note that the Product neutrality function does not accurately predict model fitnesses well for beneficial mutations—that is, mutations that increase growth rate (see Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in appendix figure.

claim: The Weiße model incorporates nutrient intake, transcription, competitive binding between mRNAs and ribosomes, and translation, all mediated by associated enzymes and a limiting cellular 'energy'.
source: Here, we consider the model of Weiße et al., 2015, which incorporates nutrient intake, transcription, competitive binding between mRNAs and ribosomes, and translation, all of which are mediated by associated enzymes and a limiting cellular 'energy' (Figure 4A).
evidence: Description of the Weiße model structure.

claim: The Weiße model explicitly models four types of proteins: transport proteins, metabolic enzymes, ribosomal proteins, and q-proteins which support housekeeping functions.
source: Four types of proteins are explicitly modeled as a product of translation: transport proteins, metabolic enzymes, ribosomal proteins, and so-called q-proteins which support housekeeping functions much like the 'other' proteins in the Scott–Hwa model.
evidence: Description of the Weiße model structure.

claim: The Product neutrality function is generally better than the Additive or Minimal neutrality functions at describing the mutational results in the Weiße model.
source: Our mutational analysis of the Weiße model revealed several striking observations. First, the Product neutrality function is generally better than the Additive or Minimal neutrality functions at describing the mutational results.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of the Weiße model.

claim: Parameter pairs involving protein translation in the Weiße model follow the Scott-Hwa model very closely.
source: The subset of parameter pairs involving protein translation follows the Scott–Hwa model very closely (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in figure.

claim: Parameter pairs involving mutations to transport, metabolism, and transcription sectors in the Weiße model follow the Product neutrality function even more closely than the Scott-Hwa model.
source: On the other hand, another subset of parameter pairs follows the Product neutrality function even more closely. These parameter pairs involve mutations to the other sectors, including the transport, metabolism, and transcription sectors (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in figure.

claim: In the Weiße model, the amplitude of deviation from the Product neutrality function is governed by the inverse of the Michaelis-Menten constant giving the transcription rate as a function of the cellular 'energy'.
source: Second, the amplitude of deviation from the Product neutrality function is governed by an additional parameter, γ, which is the inverse of the Michaelis–Menten constant giving the transcription rate as a function of the cellular 'energy'.
evidence: Derived from analytical approximation of the Weiße model.

claim: Deviations from the Product neutrality function in the Weiße model can be driven by nonlinear effects, such as those that emerge from Michaelis-Menten kinetics.
source: Taken together, our analysis of the Weiße model shows how the Product neutrality function naturally arises for many different parameter pairs and how deviations from it can be driven by nonlinear effects, such as those that can emerge from Michaelis–Menten kinetics.
evidence: Conclusion from analytical and computational analysis of the Weiße model.

claim: The Product neutrality function was shown to better predict double-mutant fitnesses than an Additive neutrality function and a Minimum neutrality function in previous work (Mani et al., 2008).
source: This neutrality function was shown to better predict double-mutant fitnesses than an Additive neutrality function, where the differences between wild-type and mutant fitnesses were simply added together, and a Minimum neutrality function, where the double-mutant fitness was taken as the lowest fitness of the two single-mutant strains.
evidence: Reference to previous work by Mani et al., 2008.

claim: Genetic analyses rely on a neutrality function that predicts the expected phenotype for double mutants based on the phenotypes of the two individual non-interacting mutations.
source: Such analyses rely on a neutrality function that predicts the expected phenotype for double mutants based on the phenotypes of the two individual non-interacting mutations.
evidence: General statement about genetic analysis methodology.

claim: A genetic interaction is identified when combining multiple mutations yields something unexpected.
source: In other words, a genetic interaction is identified when combining multiple mutations yields something unexpected.
evidence: Definition of genetic interaction.

claim: The neutrality function calculates the expected phenotype of a double-mutant strain carrying two non-interacting mutations (Beltrao et al., 2010; Mani et al., 2008).
source: In this way, the neutrality function calculates the expected phenotype of a double-mutant strain carrying two non-interacting mutations (Beltrao et al., 2010; Mani et al., 2008).
evidence: Definition supported by citations.

claim: The neutrality function should be defined such that most mutations are categorized as non-interacting.
source: The neutrality function should be defined such that most mutations are categorized as non-interacting.
evidence: Principle for defining neutrality functions.

claim: Decades of cell biological and structural biological analysis have identified specific functions for many genes and their associated proteins.
source: However, decades of cell biological and structural biological analysis have identified specific functions for many genes and their associated proteins.
evidence: General statement about the state of biological knowledge.

claim: A judiciously selected neutrality function should predict most double-mutant fitnesses from the single-mutant fitnesses since any two randomly selected genes should be unlikely to interact.
source: This implies that a judiciously selected neutrality function should predict most double-mutant fitnesses from the single-mutant fitnesses since any two randomly selected genes should be unlikely to interact.
evidence: Logical inference from the specificity of gene functions.

claim: Synthetic Genetic Arrays (SGAs) have generated the largest and most comprehensive datasets of single and double genetic mutants in budding yeast (Baryshnikova et al., 2010b; Costanzo et al., 2010; Costanzo et al., 2016).
source: In budding yeast, Synthetic Genetic Arrays (SGAs) Tong et al., 2001 have generated the largest and most comprehensive such datasets (Baryshnikova et al., 2010b; Costanzo et al., 2010; Costanzo et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about the SGA dataset supported by citations.

claim: Fitness is defined as the relative exponential growth rate with respect to that of a wild-type cell.
source: Here, we focus on this property and define fitness as the relative exponential growth rate with respect to that of a wild-type cell.
evidence: Definition of fitness used in the study.

claim: For yeast proliferation, single-mutant fitnesses are usually assumed to combine according to a Product neutrality function (Mani et al., 2008).
source: For yeast proliferation, single-mutant fitnesses are usually assumed to combine according to a Product neutrality function, namely that the fitness of the double mutant is the product of the fitnesses of the single mutants (Mani et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement about common assumption supported by citation.

claim: The SGA data are from combinations of gene deletions, temperature-sensitive alleles, and hypomorphic mutants.
source: We note that these data are from combinations of gene deletions, temperature-sensitive alleles, and hypomorphic mutants (see Methods).
evidence: Description of the types of mutations in the SGA dataset.

claim: Cells in the SGA experiments were growing quickly on relatively rich synthetic complete media containing glucose (Baryshnikova et al., 2010a).
source: Moreover, cells were growing quickly on the relatively rich synthetic complete media containing glucose (Baryshnikova et al., 2010a).
evidence: Description of experimental conditions supported by citation.

claim: In the SGA experiments, mutations generally decrease fitness.
source: For these reasons, increasing the growth rate is difficult, and we are in the regime where mutations generally decrease fitness.
evidence: Observation about the nature of mutations in the dataset.

claim: The observation that the cellular ribosome fraction increases with growth rate is generic and also seen in the yeast S. cerevisiae (Metzl-Raz et al., 2017; Elsemman et al., 2022; Xia et al., 2022).
source: Experimental measurements in other organisms suggest that the observations leading to this model, including that the cellular ribosome fraction increases with growth rate, are in fact generic and also seen in the yeast S. cerevisiae (Metzl-Raz et al., 2017; Elsemman et al., 2022; Xia et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental measurements in yeast.

claim: The Product neutrality function naturally emerges from both the Scott-Hwa and Weiße growth models due to the interdependence of cellular processes that maximize growth rates.
source: We perform a computational genetic analysis to show that in both models, the Product neutrality function naturally emerges due to the interdependence of cellular processes that maximize growth rates.
evidence: Main conclusion from computational analysis of both models.

claim: The Product neutrality function performs better than Additive or Minimum neutrality functions in describing colony growth rate data from budding yeast.
source: This Product neutrality function performs better than Additive or Minimum neutrality functions, supporting its continued use in genetic interaction studies.
evidence: Main finding from analysis of SGA data.

claim: The Product neutrality function describes the colony growth rate, or fitness, of a double mutant as the product of the fitnesses of the individual single mutants.
source: Our results confirm that the Product neutrality function describes the colony growth rate, or fitness, of a double mutant as the product of the fitnesses of the individual single mutants.
evidence: Main finding from the study.

claim: The SGA dataset has been used to assign a biological process to each gene (Costanzo et al., 2016).
source: We note that the SGA dataset has already been used to assign a biological process to each gene (Costanzo et al., 2016).
evidence: Reference to previous use of the SGA dataset.

claim: Mutations affecting the same biological process should have similar genetic interaction profiles.
source: The reasoning was that mutations affecting the same biological process should have similar genetic interaction profiles, which was found to be the case.
evidence: Reasoning used in previous analysis of SGA data.

claim: When improving the efficiency of one process in the Scott-Hwa model with beneficial mutations, proteomic resources are allocated to accelerate other processes in the cell.
source: When the Scott–Hwa model's growth-optimizing feedback operates in the context of beneficial mutations, as one process is made more efficient, proteomic resources are allocated to accelerate other processes in the cell.
evidence: Explanation of model behavior with beneficial mutations.

claim: In the Scott-Hwa model with beneficial mutations, improving the efficiency of one process will indirectly benefit other processes, leading to compound effects such that double-mutant fitnesses are higher than any of the three models predicts.
source: In this way, improving the efficiency of one process will indirectly benefit other processes, leading to compound effects such that double-mutant fitnesses are higher than any of the three models predicts for beneficial mutations.
evidence: Explanation of model behavior with beneficial mutations.
